intro.text: eylem eylül acarsoy. eylosh, for short.
a researcher and designer who never managed to stay in one discipline.
she is curious about how identity, expression and introspection are shaped by the societies and institutions around us.
she studied visual communication design with a strong dose of cultural studies, and spent a few years in sociology too. one taught her to make things, the other to ask why people do what they do.
she has run cultural and educational spaces and organisations, coordinated projects and events, facilitated workshops, built archives, and gave art, research and organisations a visual voice.
today she is a master's candidate in the social and public innovation cluster at KISD in cologne, and a research assistant at the university of wuppertal.
she looks at things from six sides:
intro.then: she loves solutions, but she doesn't rush them.

intro.text: she feels most at home in community. these days that's the hidden agenda collective: artists and designers from many fields.
also: her family's home is a sanctuary for adopted stray cats. nine of them, currently.

works.title: the]institute]of[inner[mechanics
works.tag: Master Thesis · Speculative Design · Research through Design
works.question: How can design fiction become an environment for collective research?
works.text: A speculative–empirical design research project that uses a fictional institute as a shared research environment to investigate how creative learning environments can support introspection, metacognition and self-authorship, through participatory workshops, visual tools and collective inquiry. Moving through many creative, educational and social environments, I noticed how differently they shape the way people think, create and express themselves. I traced this through pedagogy, philosophy, psychology and sociology, and revisited earlier experiments such as Feely Thingies and Re-fin(d)ing KISD. With a "Critical Worlding Method", I designed a fictional research institute that participants enter as co-researchers, with its own identity, visual language, roles, badges, protocols, case files and research tools. Case File 00.01 took place online on a shared Miro board; Case File 00.02 translated the framework into a physical, performative workshop at KISD. The Institute is now becoming an interactive exhibition for January 2027.
works.role: Concept, research, speculative world-building, workshop design and facilitation, visual tools
works.context_line: Master thesis at KISD, Cologne. Speculative design, participatory and performative methods, research through design.

credits.with: supervised by Prof. Oliver Baron & Diego Alatorre Guzmán

works.title: memo
works.tag: Interactive Game Experience · Designing DataXCultures, KISD
works.question: How do smart technologies and AI companions influence our relationships with personal data, privacy and trust?
works.text: Imagine Cologne in 2076. A person is searching for their lost robotic dog, accompanied by an AI companion, and the city reveals itself through different layers of information. As a teaching assistant in KISD's Designing Data Cultures course, I contributed to research and discussions on smart cities, urban data infrastructures and how location-based technologies and AI companions shape the way we experience and navigate cities. This research inspired memo, a speculative educational game I co-developed with Jihyun and Texas State University. Two players wear modified red-and-blue 3D glasses, and each sees a different visual layer on the same screen; to follow the story and find the dog, they have to exchange information and combine their perspectives. Through this playful mechanic we explored data visibility, digital literacy, privacy and trust in future urban environments, and presented the prototype at an exhibition where visitors played it together.
works.role: Teaching assistance, research, game co-design
works.context_line: A speculative two-player game, developed through research and teaching assistance in the Designing DataXCultures course at KISD, with Texas State University.

works.title: Refin(d)ing KISD
works.question: How can embodying personal experiences through creative practices open up new ways of reflection?
works.text: A student-led research and intervention project on identity, belonging and community at KISD. It started with one question: what does it mean to be a KISDie? We co-founded the Re-fin(d)ing KISD Collective, listened to students through a survey, gave the answers a visual language, and turned what we learned into a playful workshop where students and professors talked about KISD together for the first time in this format.
works.role: Co-founder and co-lead of the collective; research, workshop design and facilitation
works.context_line: A Master and Self-Initiated Project (MIP/SIP) at KISD, Cologne, supervised by Diego Alatorre Guzmán.

credits.with: with the Re-fin(d)ing KISD Collective: Annalena, Alina, Citra, Thilini, Moritz, Levin, Jonas, Sofia, Zoe, Samuel and many more

bullets.title: what I did
items: Co-founded the Re-fin(d)ing KISD Collective and co-led it within the lead team.
Helped run the student survey on belonging and KISD's identity, and make sense of the answers together.
Worked on the collective's visual language and communication: the "How it feels to be a KISDie" visualisation, posters and the call to join.
Co-designed and co-facilitated the Designer Identity Doll workshop on 20 January 2026, from the doll-making to the discussion with professors.
Documented the process and reflected on it in a course report.

sections.title: where it started
sections.text: It began in the Re-thinking Design Education long-term project in 2025 with Prof. Oliver Baron and Diego Alatorre Guzmán, where we talked about education, design education, best practices and creativity. It became the Re-thinking / Transforming Design Education AG, a working group trying to understand KISD's problems and intervene. From there, some of us started the Re-fin(d)ing KISD Collective, around three questions: what does it mean to be a KISDie, is there a problem with community at KISD, and who is responsible for it?

sections.title: listening: the survey
sections.text: In the summer term of 2025 we asked students what they love, experience and wish for at KISD: about values, atmosphere, responsibility and possible changes. There was strong appreciation for freedom, but also recurring feelings of being lost, disconnected or unsupported. These answers defined the core tensions we kept working with.

sections.title: how it feels to be a KISDie
sections.text: We turned the answers into a visualisation of six themes: attitudes and mindsets, moments and rituals, spaces and objects, care and trace, learning and autonomy, support and belonging. Its visual language is fluid and playful on purpose: it shows many identities rather than one fixed KISD.

flow.caption: "How it feels to be a KISDie": scroll inside the image ↓

sections.title: from a working group to a collective
sections.text: We presented our insights at the Friday Presentations and invited everyone to join; a WhatsApp community grew from there. The initiative became a Master and Self-Initiated Project, supervised by Diego Alatorre Guzmán. A small lead team collected and refined ideas, open weekly meetings brought in more voices, and we looked back at the history of KISD and the Kölner Modell to understand where its freedom comes from. Working with Diego, we decided to approach heavy topics through play.

flow.caption: Things that we can change at KISD: four themes from the survey and open talks
The plan: discussions, workshops and a SIP incubator

sections.title: designing the workshop
sections.text: Instead of trying to fix the institution, we designed a format where students could articulate their own position within it. At its core was the Designer Identity Doll: each participant built a doll in two halves, one for their current designer identity (skills, habits, interests) and one for their struggles, insecurities, stereotypes and fears about the future. Colour cards paired people randomly, outside their friend groups, and guiding prompts helped each pair describe the other's designer identity.

sections.title: the workshop day
sections.text: On 20 January 2026, the workshop moved from making to talking: paired exchanges, a sharing circle where everyone presented their doll, and a question matrix on the floor. Its two axes asked whether participants feel supported by KISD (receiving) and whether they feel able to change it (giving); placing the dolls on it made the group's sense of support and agency visible at a glance.

flow.caption: The question matrix: giving and receiving

sections.title: talking with the faculty
sections.text: For the final circle we invited professors and staff with different perspectives: Mr. Wrede on the original vision of KISD, Daniela on its structures and organisation, Sebastian as a newer professor, and Jule as a former student and current research assistant. We started with a personal question, what is your relationship with KISD?, and the conversation moved to self-responsibility and neglect, freedom and structure, identity and community. It was the first dialogue of this kind between students and faculty.

sections.title: what came out of it
sections.text: As a first workshop in this format, it had no predefined outcome: it tested whether students and professors are willing to have these conversations, and they were. At the end we asked everyone what the values of KISD are, what feels clear and what still seems abstract. Their answers became the starting points for what comes next.

sections.title: looking back
sections.text: I had just arrived in Germany from Türkiye and was trying to understand a new educational system and a new culture. The collective became part of my own integration: a way to connect, to meet people and to take initiative in a place whose values I care about. It was the first time I truly felt autonomy, agency and active learning in a university project, intellectually, socially and emotionally. It also showed me how much agency students at KISD have, and how open the institution is to questioning itself. I believe that ability, to reflect critically and keep reconfiguring from within, is one of the most valuable things an organisation can have.

works.title: Motif
works.tag: Critical Design · Tangible Interaction · Graduation Project
works.question: What happens when a society gets stuck in its search for originality?
works.text: An independent speculative design and tangible interaction project exploring technology, identity and consumer culture through an interactive fictional world. What happens when a society gets stuck in its search for originality? Motif imagines an island society where people increasingly rely on machines to construct and maintain their individuality, told from the machines' point of view. Visitors discover the island by placing physical Motif disks into a tangible storytelling console; each disk reveals a fragment of the story, in any order. I built the interaction with Arduino, sensors and projection mapping, and developed a visual language through PETSCII animations. During the pandemic, Motif became my creative playground and sparked my interest in tangible interfaces, interaction logic and narrative.
works.role: Concept · storytelling · interaction design · tangible prototyping · installation
works.tools: Arduino · Processing · 3D printing · laser-cut cardboard · projection mapping
works.context_line: Graduation project at Yaşar University, shown at Good Design ÜTAŞ 2021.

review.text: I engaged in philosophical debates about Motif's nature, leading me towards critical design. The project contained compelling elements of system design, nudging me towards service design within its narrative. My presentation of Motif was methodological, systematic, and comprehensive.

works.question: How do people feel about bureaucracy before they even arrive?
works.text: A team project with the City of Cologne, researching and redesigning services for the Kundenzentrum. works.question: What does trustworthy news look like in 2040?
works.text: By 2040, fake news and information bubbles dominate and traditional media is losing relevance. As the innovation team of a media corporation, we reimagined the future of news and a strategy for trustworthy journalism. Our answer: an interactive media literacy detective play kit for children, tangible and digital, distributed through health insurance companies and designed to promote critical thinking through play. Methods included opportunity framing, influence loops, a client journey and a north star metric.

works.title: Urla Design Library
works.question: How can a 500-year-old school building become a library where ideas never stop moving?
works.context_line: Visual identity for Urla Design Library, in a restored 16th-century Ottoman primary school. Yaşar University, VCDS 4101.
works.text: Urla Design Library lives in a stone building with a dome, once an Ottoman primary school, restored by Prof. Dr. Tevfik Balcıoğlu. Through research and a research booklet on the library and Ottoman primary schools, the concept of udl took shape: a social, active, productive place where thoughts are constantly passed on. The motto "thoughts through arches" plays on "through ages": the arches of the building become the visual system, standing side by side like the people they connect.
works.role: Research, concept, visual identity, stationery, research booklet, web mock-up

works.text: A social, sharable and customisable interactive experience: a serious game with a historical narrative generated according to the visitor's personality type, cognitive style and visitor type. Selected projects, including this one, were exhibited at Good Design.

works.title: Diffilterly
works.question: Can a toy be genderless, anti-bully and eco-friendly at the same time?
works.context_line: A cardboard toy for 8 to 12 year olds. Yaşar University, VCDS 2252 Creative Thinking in Design.
works.text: Research and a persona showed that children aged 8 to 12 want to create, combine, collect and share, and to carry what they make. Diffilterly lets them do all of it. Laser-cut cardboard keeps it neutral and ecological; a Cubism-inspired style stands for embracing all people. A metal plate holds magnetic pieces and the top works as a canvas. The name comes from different + filter; the logo's eye, the most genderless feature of the body, wears differently coloured lashes.
works.role: Research, persona, product and brand design (team project)

review.text: This project's social insight was invaluable to me. Though not explicitly stated in the brief, I focused on social and innovative elements in my designs, showcasing my respect for diversity. It also enhanced my product design skills and sparked a passion for material experimentation.

credits.with: with Merve Topay

works.title: Contact Film Festival Archive
works.question: How can a film archive be explored by someone who cannot see the screen?
works.context_line: A blind-friendly, sound-based kiosk archive for Contact Film Festival at Yaşar University. VCDS 3101.
works.text: A research-driven, blind-friendly, sound-based interactive kiosk interface for the international Contact Film Festival. Its cyberpunk lens reflects the festival's young audience; users explore the archive with different filters on a large screen. Comparative research, a 2x2 matrix, a provisional persona and accessibility research, together with creative sound design, made it a blind-friendly interface.
works.role: UX research, interface and sound design (team project)

review.text: In this project, while not initially focused on accessibility, I deliberately integrated it, marking my first foray into the field. Deciphering complex information was developmental, but if I were to redo it for the visually impaired today, I would opt for a more minimalistic approach.

credits.with: with Zeynep Güneş Acar

works.title: wHH0
works.question: What would a game look like if you could only keep walking?
works.context_line: A story-driven platform game concept. Yaşar University, VCDS 3102.
works.text: wHH0 allegorically handles self, alienation, depersonalisation, derealisation and climate change. Waking up in a hot, dry world, wHH0 hides from the Unaware DROs and sets off towards HusHHusH with the resistance network of Aware DROs. wHH0 cannot jump, run or fight: it has to stay hidden, silent and keep walking through heat loss and self-alienation. No menus, no inventory bars, no score. You walk, and you don't give up.
works.role: Story, world and visual concept (team project)

credits.with: with Merve Topay & Zeynep Güneş Acar

works.title: F Fanzine
works.question: What does it feel like to never quite fit the box you are given?
works.context_line: Ata Kam's fanzine workshop in the scope of F Project, on "being a copy", using photocopy.
works.text: The glitches that photocopying brings to my long-distance bus tickets became the material: data that never fits its sections, like the student passenger who never finds her place. Those were my tickets, from years of travelling between Milas, Söke and İzmir. The zoomed glitches were sorted by kind and stapled to feel like a ticket, and the fanzine was bound with a Japanese stitch taught by Ata Kam. Exhibited in Diyarbakır, Ankara and İzmir.
works.role: Concept, photocopy imagery, binding

review.text: In this workshop, I initially created from a deeply personal perspective, but upon reflection, I realized my artistry leans towards socially grounded works, making my initial attempts feel overly personal in hindsight.

credits.with: with Ata Kam, coord. Umut Altıntaş

works.title: Kemeraltı Dictionary
works.question: What does the street language of a bazaar say about the people who write it?
works.context_line: A process-oriented workshop on oral culture in İzmir's Kemeraltı Bazaar, Good Design 2018.
works.text: We spent a whole day in Kemeraltı Bazaar, photographing everything, talking with people and exploring places and objects. A pattern appeared in the written language of the shops: ironic, surreal sentences on banners, with spelling mistakes and imperative forms. We collected them, chose the ones that best carry the bazaar's culture, and turned them into stickers with a young visual language.
works.role: Field research, typography, sticker design (collective workshop)

review.text: This workshop introduced me to Izmir's cultural hub for the first time, highlighting my interest in oral culture. All projects were co-created, and the workshop's fluid flow greatly influenced my approach and focus.

works.title: Balcony Balustrades of Ankara
works.tag: Scientific Research Project · Interaction Design · Exhibition
works.question: How can digital tools help us see, compare and keep an architectural heritage that is disappearing?
works.context_line: Interactive Digital Exhibits to Experience Architectural Heritage: The Case of Balcony Balustrades of Ankara (1950–1975). A Yaşar University scientific research project (BAP086), exhibited at the İzmir Architecture Center, 5–28 July 2021.
works.text: A scientific research project at the meeting point of architectural history and interaction design. Balcony balustrades are one of the most visible elements of Ankara's modern apartment architecture between 1950 and 1975, yet they are scattered across the city, rarely seen side by side, and disappear quickly as the urban fabric changes. The project documented a collection of around 2,000 balustrades, mapped them to their locations and turned the collection into an interactive digital exhibit, so that people could explore, filter and compare them.
works.role: Interface design, exhibition setup, photography and video, social media

review.text: I contributed to this project during the exhibition setup, managing the UI/UX and social media aspects. It was one of my first experiences with exhibition installation, providing an opportunity to apply my knowledge in interaction design to reality.

credits.with: coord. Assoc. Prof. Zeynep Tuna Ultav, with Daniele Savasta and Gökhan Keskin

bullets.title: what I did
items: Designed the interface of the interactive database app that visitors used on their phones to explore the collection and control the projected exhibition map, under the supervision of Daniele Savasta.
Took part in setting up the exhibition at the İzmir Architecture Center: the floor map, the QR codes and the exhibition graphics.
Photographed and filmed the opening of the exhibition.
Edited the project trailer and the thumbnails of the interview series.
Designed and managed the project's social media.

sections.title: the research
sections.text: The project treats balcony balustrades as architectural ephemera: elements we usually see as lasting, yet in a rapidly transforming city they vanish within a short time, together with the memories and socio-cultural references they carry. Photographing, classifying and mapping the balustrades preserves them as a digital collection and makes their role in shaping the image of neighbourhoods visible.

sections.title: from collection to data
sections.text: The balustrades were photographed across Ankara's neighbourhoods and classified by region, neighbourhood and category. The data were first mapped to their geographical positions with geojson, which was then used to view and filter the collection, and illustrated as a typology of balustrade drawings.

sections.title: the app and the exhibition
sections.text: In the exhibition, a map of Ankara's neighbourhoods was taped onto the floor with QR codes for the balustrades, and a large projection showed the collection on the city map. Visitors used a mobile web app to browse regions, neighbourhoods, categories and illustrations, and their choices appeared on the projection.

sections.title: publication
sections.text: The project was presented in the paper "Visualizing Architectural Ephemera: The Case of Ankara Balcony Balustrades 1950–75" at the Sixteenth International Conference on Design Principles & Practices (19–21 January 2022, University of Newcastle, Australia). It discusses how a digital collection is translated into a computational interface for studying collections, called Grouper, through a speculative realism lens.

systems.text: eylül learned systems by running them. with ARAMA she coordinated {{giy|GİY}}, an education platform for students; at {{bayetav|BAYETAV Art}} she went from running events to shaping how the whole space worked. now she maps learning paths into a tool at the university of wuppertal: {{lernpfad|Lernpfad-Designer}}.

learning.text: it started with a course in applied drama: learning by doing. at {{giy|GİY}} she designed learning materials and workshops for students, and her thesis {{inner-mechanics|the institute of inner mechanics}} asks how creative education can make room for introspection. today she builds {{lernpfad|Lernpfad-Designer}} at the university of wuppertal.

visual.text: visual communication design was her first language, and she still speaks it every day. since 2019 she has designed identities, publications and websites as a freelancer, and the {{publications|reports and books}} of BAYETAV. her way of working: understanding complexity → structuring ideas → visualizing clarity.

art.text: she makes things by hand, usually with others: letterpress at {{fuar-matbaasi|Fuar Matbaası}}, an installation like {{motif|Motif}}, exhibitions at BAYETAV Art. today her small studio is at the Hidden Agenda Collective, among artists and designers from many fields. at KISD she builds speculative worlds, like {{inner-mechanics|a fictional institute}}.

research.text: cultural studies came first, then fieldwork in places like {{abacioglu|Abacıoğlu Han}}, then a few years of sociology. at KISD she studies how people trust public data in {{cologne|Customer Centers of the Future}} and how education feels from the inside in {{refinding-kisd|Refin(d)ing KISD}}. for her, data is never just technical: it is cultural, emotional and human.

approach.title: how she works
approach.sub: keep scrolling. she walks around a project before she touches it.

steps.label: critical
steps.text: first, she asks why it is like this, and who decided that it should be.

steps.label: speculative
steps.text: then she imagines it otherwise. what if?

steps.label: empathetic
steps.text: she listens to the people it is for, before she draws anything.

steps.label: hands-on
steps.text: she makes it real and tests it with real people, in real places.

steps.label: detail-oriented
steps.text: she goes through every detail, and weaves it back together.

steps.label: honest
steps.text: she shows what happened, including what did not work.

approach.summary: six ways of looking, one project at a time.

cv.bio: Eylem Eylül Acarsoy is a transdisciplinary researcher and designer exploring how identity, expression, and introspection are shaped within societal and institutional structures. With a background in visual communication, ranging from editorial and exhibition design to social media and digital platforms, she brings a holistic and systemic approach to design. Her experience spans managing cultural and educational institutions, facilitating participatory formats, and building archives and communication strategies across art, research, and organizational contexts. She is deeply curious about the ways people connect, learn, and transform together, and often finds herself nourished by the dynamics of community, collaboration, and shared rituals. She asks a lot of questions, laughs a lot, and is happiest when a room full of people starts making something together.
